THIRD-PARTY NOTICES

Portals (https://portals-endless-worlds.netlify.app) builds on the open-source
work listed here. Thank you to its authors.

The first four are distributed under the MIT License. Each has its own
copyright line below; the licence text that follows them applies to each.


1. three.js (release 170) and its addons
   The 3D library the whole site is drawn with.
   https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js

   Copyright © 2010-2024 three.js authors

   One world's own file (the plan of the otter airliner) measures the
   distance from a point to a triangle with a function that follows
   Triangle.closestPointToPoint of three.js. The three.js source says of
   that method: "algorithm thanks to Real-Time Collision Detection by
   Christer Ericson, published by Morgan Kaufmann Publishers, (c) 2005
   Elsevier Inc., under the accompanying license; see chapter 5.1.5 for
   detailed explanation." That credit is passed on here as three.js gives
   it; no terms beyond the three.js licence are claimed.

   One world's own files (floor-without-windows) carry the five numbers of
   the filmic tone curve that three.js applies in its
   ACESFilmicToneMapping, a fit of the ACES curve by Stephen Hill as
   three.js carries it. The world runs that curve backwards, so that a
   colour reaches the screen as it was chosen. The numbers are taken from
   three.js; the credit for the fit is passed on here as the world's makers
   gave it; no terms beyond the three.js licence are claimed.


2. Hash without Sine
   Sine-free hash functions for shaders: hash11, hash12, hash13, hash22 and
   hash33 in this site's shader kit and engine, and the same functions where
   a world's own shader carries them. One world's own script
   (pallet-tower-midsummer) carries a variant of them in plain arithmetic,
   with the same numbers.
   https://www.shadertoy.com/view/4djSRW

   Copyright (c)2014 David Hoskins.


3. webgl-noise
   Simplex noise for shaders: snoise in this site's shader kit.
   https://github.com/ashima/webgl-noise

   Copyright (C) 2011 by Ashima Arts (Simplex noise)
   Copyright (C) 2011-2016 by Stefan Gustavson (Classic noise and others)


4. Shader functions by Inigo Quilez
   Three short functions follow code published by this author. The exact
   distance to a box in the plane (sdBox in the portal, i_box in this site's
   interior kit, and the same function where a world's own shader carries
   it). The polynomial smooth minimum in the terrain kit. The value noise in
   three dimensions read from one 256 by 256 noise texture, whose two
   channels are the same field shifted by a fixed pair of numbers, so that
   one lookup gives two layers (vn3 in this site's sky kit, and the same
   function where a world's own shader carries it); this one is known from
   the author's shaders rather than from an article. Three more stand in
   one world's own code, the statue of the Colossus of Rhodes: the distances
   to a round cone between two points, to an ellipsoid and to a box with
   rounded edges, as the author's article on distance functions in three
   dimensions gives them (iquilezles.org, article distfunctions). The
   author's site says that its code that implements an algorithm is under
   the MIT License.
   https://iquilezles.org/articles/distfunctions2d/
   https://iquilezles.org/articles/smin/
   https://www.shadertoy.com/user/iq

   Copyright (c) Inigo Quilez

ALSO WITH THANKS

Short, widely published forms that this site uses, named here as a courtesy:

- mulberry32, a small random number generator, in the form widely attributed
  to Tommy Ettinger. It stands in this site's sound engine, in its portal
  code, in its kit for skies, ground and animals, and in the own files of
  twenty-two of its worlds. No licence statement for it has been found, so
  no terms are claimed here; it is named because its authorship is known.

- The sine hash, in the form fract(sin(dot(p, c)) * 43758.5453) and its
  one-, two- and three-number variants, with the constants usually published
  with it (12.9898 and 78.233, or 127.1 and 311.7, inside the sine, the
  large multiplier shown above, and in some two-number variants a triple such as 123.34 with 345.45
  and 34.345, or 123.34 with 456.21 and 45.32). It is the oldest way to make a random
  number in a shader and it is published in hundreds of places. It stands in
  this site's shader kit and in its engine, and in the own files of most of
  its worlds: by a count made on 14 October 2026, 429 files carry the form
  and 178 of those carry one of the triples named above. No author and no
  licence statement for the form could be established, so no author is named
  and no terms are claimed. It is listed here because the site brings it in,
  and because it is the constants as much as the shape that are the
  published thing. Readers of this project's own code believe that the two
  triples above follow one author's published shaders; that could not be
  confirmed from any page, so this notice makes no claim about it. The site
  ships its source unbuilt and readable, so every line that uses the form
  can be read.

- A closed form for the share of a normal (bell) curve that lies below a
  given point, written as a logistic of a cubic, after Bowling, Khasawneh,
  Kaewkuekool and Cho, "A logistic approximation to the cumulative normal
  distribution", Journal of Industrial Engineering and Management 2 (1),
  2009, pages 114 to 127. One line in the own file of one world
  (pallet-tower-midsummer) is written anew from that idea, with the two
  numbers that the form gives to anyone who fits it. A formula is
  mathematics, so no terms are claimed; the article is named here as a
  courtesy.
